name: Tomas Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a four-man bucket-truck crew out of the depot in Kessel Valley, mostly rural distribution lines for the regional power company. We're in the yard at quarter to seven, I hand out the paper job packs, we do the tailboard talk about the hazards, then it's poles, crossarms, transformers, whatever's broken or due. I love the bit where you're up in the bucket and the whole valley is quiet under you. What wears me out is the storm call-outs, sixteen hours in the rain and then back in the yard at seven the next morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the job pay for at home, and who's there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Lena, my partner, she's a nurse on the night ward at the district hospital. We rent a flat above the bakery on Mill Street, so I smell bread when I get home from a storm shift. We've got about four months of money put away, and we're trying to build it up before we think about buying. I'm twenty-seven and I made crew lead last spring, which is young for our depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Fine by me, honestly, I've never touched one of those chat things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the depot I'd say I told you so, loudly, over the kettle. The office lot kept sending emails about digital this and smart that, and we still end up hanging off a pole with a hot stick. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union about how the real work still needs real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's as safe as it ever was, which is pretty safe. The grid is old, the storms are getting worse, and there aren't enough of us. Nobody's going to write an app that climbs a rotten pole in a gale, and the power company knows it. My worry would still be the same one I have now, that management keeps the crews too thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Keep putting a few hundred a month into savings so Lena and I can get a deposit together in maybe three years. I'd keep pushing at union meetings for a fifth person on the storm rota, because that's the fight that actually matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. It's nice to picture a world where the thing everyone panicked about turned out to be a fancy spellchecker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thin crews are the real worry. What does that look like on a bad night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February we had three of us on a broken pole at two in the morning because the fourth was off sick and nobody would pay for cover. Marco, our youngest, was shaking from the cold by the end. That's when someone gets hurt, not because of a computer but because of a spreadsheet in head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, where do you see yourself in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same depot, maybe a supervisor if old Piet ever retires. Lena and me in a little house with a garden, ideally near the river. That's the whole plan, and in this picture it's a plan that works.

say: I'd tell the depot the **digital hype** never touched real line work.
I'd share **union posts** saying the grid still needs real people up the poles.
think: My job feels **as safe as ever** because the grid is old and crews are short.
My real worry stays **thin crews**, which come from management decisions, not computers.
do: Keep **saving a few hundred** a month toward a house deposit in about three years.
Push at **union meetings** for a fifth person on the storm rota.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with a bit of smugness about the hype fading.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to write an app that climbs a rotten pole in a gale, and the power company knows it.
fieldNote: He has **never used AI** and sees office tech talk as a distraction from safety.
His anger points at **head office budgets**, not machines; the cold February night is his reference story.
Steady pay, a nurse partner and some savings make this world feel **secure** to him.

steps.text: Put a few hundred a month into the house deposit fund
Keep leading the Kessel Valley crew on the same routes
Argue at union meetings for a fifth person on storm call-outs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. Planning and booking, that's half of what the office does for us. Go on, I'm listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office jobs are in trouble, but you still can't send a chatbot up a pole. To the lads I'd say keep your heads down and keep your tickets current. Online I'd back the union calling for any savings to go into more crews, not shareholder payouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gets closer to me than I'd like. The job packs, the switching plans and the call-out rota would all come from software, and I hate apps. I'd be the crew lead who has to read everything off a tablet instead of a piece of paper I can fold into my pocket. I'm not scared for the climbing, I'm scared of becoming slow at the part of my job that isn't climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask the union rep to get tablet training done on paid time, not on our evenings. I'd ask Marco to show me the new screens, since he's twenty-two and lives on his phone. I'd keep saving like before, but I'd hold off on the house for a year to see whether overtime gets cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, just that feeling when the ground's a bit soft under your boots. I've spent nine years getting good at reading a pole, and now I'd have to get good at reading a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the depot would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa in dispatch, definitely. She's the one who knows which farmer has a bad dog and which lane floods. If the computer does the rota, she's gone, and we lose all that knowledge with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the house. What would make you go ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If after a year my overtime is still there and nobody's talking about cutting crews, we'd go for it. Overtime is maybe a fifth of my pay in a stormy year. If that shrinks because a computer plans the jobs tighter, the deposit plan slips.

say: I'd say **office jobs** are in trouble, but nobody sends a chatbot up a pole.
I'd back the union demand that **savings fund crews**, not shareholder payouts.
think: The **job packs and rota** moving to software touches me more than I'd like.
I fear getting **slow at the paperwork** side, not losing the climbing.
do: Ask the union rep for **tablet training** on paid time.
Get Marco, the youngest lineman, to show him the **new screens**.
Delay the **house purchase** a year to check whether overtime shrinks.
feel: **Uneasy**, like soft ground under his boots, but not frightened.
S1.quote: I've spent nine years getting good at reading a pole, and now I'd have to get good at reading a tablet.
fieldNote: He sees the threat as **losing skill status**, not losing the job itself.
He worries for **Rosa in dispatch**, whose local knowledge he values over any software.
**Overtime** is about a fifth of his pay, so tighter planning hits his house plans first.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for tablet training on paid hours
Get Marco to teach him the new job-pack screens
Put the house purchase on hold for one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not much at all. And robots by 2031, so I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say this is exactly why the grid should be in public hands, so the people who keep the lights on aren't thrown away. I'd say it at the union branch and I'd put my name on whatever petition came round. With the crew I'd keep it light, because nobody climbs well when they're scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think 2028 takes the office and 2031 takes me. The thinking side of my job, the job packs, the switching orders, the fault finding off the maps, that'd all be done by the AI straight away. Then I've got about three years of climbing left before a machine can do it. I'd be thirty-two with a diploma in a job a robot does, and I've never even used a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal: retraining money, a guarantee that crews get cut slowly, not in one go. I'd move savings up to the top of the list, cancel the car upgrade and get our cushion from four months to eight. Lena's job feels safer than mine, so we'd probably let her hours carry us while I work out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when a cable you're standing under starts humming wrong. I'd be lying awake next to Lena after her night shifts, going through numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used a chatbot. Would you start, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know that sounds stubborn. What's the point of learning the thing that's taking your job? I'd rather spend those evenings getting a second ticket in something hands-on, maybe heat pumps, even though the robots come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night the news really lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not buying the house, not yet. And I'd say I'm sorry, because I always told her line work was the one job they could never take away. She'd probably tell me to stop being dramatic and go to sleep.

say: I'd say this proves the grid belongs in **public hands**.
I'd sign every **union petition** and keep it light with my crew.
think: I expect **2028 takes the office** work and 2031 takes my climbing.
I'd have about **three years** of climbing left before robots match me.
do: Push the union for a deal with **retraining money** and slow, staged crew cuts.
Cancel the car upgrade and grow **savings to eight months**.
Lean on **Lena's nursing income** while working out a next step.
feel: **Sick** and awake at night, running numbers next to his partner.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-two with a diploma in a job a robot does, and I've never even used a chatbot.
fieldNote: He sees a clear sequence: **paperwork first**, then the climbing three years later.
He refuses to learn AI, framing it as **learning your replacement**.
He blames **private ownership** and pushes public control as the answer.
His apology to Lena shows **pride** tied up in the job's safety.

steps.text: Push the union branch for retraining money and staged crew cuts
Cancel the car upgrade and build savings to eight months
Rely on Lena's nursing pay while he plans a next step
Sign petitions for public ownership of the grid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots around 2034. That's more like it, but still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union has five years to get a proper deal, so stop wasting them. At work I'd tell the crew this is the time to get every certificate going while the company still pays for courses. Online I'd share stuff about a jobs guarantee for grid workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes it for me. The paperwork side goes in 2031, when I'm thirty-two, and the climbing maybe 2034, when I'm thirty-five. Five years is long enough to buy a house and short enough to lose the job that pays for it. So really I'd be deciding whether to buy at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still save hard, but I'd sit down with the union's training officer and pick one course I could stand, probably substation maintenance, since it's hands-on and inside. I'd keep working full overtime for the next three years to fatten the account. I'd tell Lena we rent for now and decide again in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more the useful kind. Like knowing a storm is three days out on the forecast. You can't stop it, but you can get the trucks ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pick a course you could stand. What's wrong with the rest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything on a screen. I tried an online safety module last year and gave up halfway through because the video kept freezing. I learn with my hands, standing next to someone who's done it twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company, if they pocket the savings. The government, if they let them. Not the engineers who build the robots, they're just doing their jobs like me.

say: I'd say the **union has five years** to win a proper deal.
I'd tell the crew to get **every certificate** while the company still pays.
think: The paperwork goes at **thirty-two** and the climbing around **thirty-five**.
The real decision is whether to **buy a house** at all.
do: Pick a **substation maintenance** course through the union training officer.
Work **full overtime** for three years to grow savings.
feel: **Anxious** in a useful way, like a storm forecast days out.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to buy a house and short enough to lose the job that pays for it.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn his alarm into **planning**, though he stays wary.
He only accepts **hands-on training**; screen courses put him off.
He blames **company and government**, not engineers, showing his union politics.

steps.text: Sign up for a substation maintenance course through the union
Take every overtime shift for three years and bank it
Keep renting above the bakery and decide on buying in 2029
Press the union branch for a grid workers' jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036 and robots in 2039. I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, at least there's time to do it properly, with the union at the table. I'd tell the crew nobody needs to panic this year. Online I'd say the same thing I always do: public grid, proper training, no one left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost normal to me. My paperwork goes in 2036 and the climbing in 2039, when I'm thirty-nine or forty. Honestly, I'd probably buy the house and do the job I love for another decade. The bit I'd worry about is that I'd get lazy and not plan, because ten years is the kind of number I'd ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house with Lena in the next two years, a small one, with a mortgage we could cover on her pay alone if we had to. I'd keep doing the job and stay active in the union. Around 2032 I'd start the substation course, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background, like a noise in the truck you keep meaning to get checked. It's there on long drives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy on a mortgage Lena could cover alone. Is that new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the AI talk changing me already. Before this I'd have stretched to the biggest place we could get. I'd pick a smaller house with a mortgage my partner Lena can pay on her nurse's wage if a robot takes my pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco, your young lineman, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's got about twelve good years, so enjoy them, save half his overtime and learn a second trade before he's thirty. He'd laugh at me. He thinks he's going to climb forever, like I did.

say: I'd say there's time to do it **properly**, with the union at the table.
I'd tell the crew **nobody needs to panic** this year.
think: Ten years feels **almost normal**, with robots arriving when I'm nearly forty.
My biggest risk is getting **lazy about planning** because ten years sounds far.
do: Buy a **small house** within two years on a mortgage Lena could carry.
Stay active in the **union** and keep doing the job.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like a noise in the truck he keeps ignoring.
S4.quote: I'd pick a smaller house with a mortgage my partner Lena can pay on her nurse's wage if a robot takes my pole.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him follow his **old plan**, trimmed for safety.
He already sizes the mortgage to **Lena's income** alone, a quiet change.
He admits he might **put off planning**, which fits his resistant streak.

steps.text: Buy a small house on a mortgage Lena's pay could cover
Keep leading the crew and attending union meetings
Start a substation maintenance course around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. Two years to the office going and five to the robots, that's no time to get a new trade when you learn the way I do. What would help is a proper deal, written down, that says crews come down slowly and the company pays for hands-on retraining in work time. I don't want a payout and a pat on the back, I want to be taught something real by someone who's done it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but if they're half as good as us and the company rushes them in, someone gets hurt. I'd want the union checking every new machine before it goes near a live line.

headlineQuote: I don't want a payout and a pat on the back, I want to be taught something real by someone who's done it.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old crew lead** on rural distribution lines who learns with his hands and has never used AI.
He lives with **Lena, a night nurse**, renting above a bakery and saving for a first house.
He blames **head office** and **private ownership** for thin crews and sees the union as his main lever.
He stays calm when AI fizzles, grows **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, and plans steadily when there's more warning.
He refuses AI tools but will accept **hands-on retraining**, like substation maintenance, if the company pays.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time for him to learn a new hands-on trade.
whatWouldHelp: A written **union deal** for slow crew cuts and paid, hands-on retraining during work time.
